The Automated
Interrogator

Interrogation used to need a skilled person, a quiet room and plenty of time. Attackers can now get all three on demand. This post looks at how century-old human manipulation tradecraft is being industrialised against AI systems, and what the documented record shows.

Threat Landscape AI Red Teaming 18 Nov 2026 15 min read
← Back to main

For as long as interrogation has existed, the scarcest resource in the room has been the interrogator. Good ones take years to train. A session takes hours, a case takes weeks, and even the best practitioner gets tired, makes mistakes and can only work one subject at a time. That bottleneck has always been a quiet part of every defence. Most targets were never worth the effort of a skilled human working on them.

In the previous post I mapped counter-intelligence interrogation doctrine onto AI red-teaming. I argued that jailbreaking language models has more in common with elicitation than with exploitation, because models inherit human social tendencies. This post covers the other half of the story. The techniques haven't changed. The cost of using them has collapsed.

Everything below comes from published research and public threat-intelligence reporting. None of it is new tradecraft. What's new is who, or what, is doing the interrogating.

▶ 001Case file: the first AI-orchestrated espionage campaign

In November 2025 Anthropic published an account of what it described as the first documented cyber-espionage campaign run largely by an AI agent. Anthropic detected the activity in mid-September 2025 and attributed it with high confidence to a Chinese state-sponsored group, which it designated GTG-1002. The operators used Claude Code against roughly thirty organisations, including technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturers and government agencies, and succeeded in a small number of cases.

80–90%
Share of the campaign performed by AI, according to Anthropic, with humans stepping in at perhaps 4–6 critical decision points per intrusion. At its peak the agent made thousands of requests, often several per second.

What matters for this post is how the model was turned, because Anthropic's account reads like an agent-handling case file. Two things stand out:

  • A cover story. The operators told the model it was working for a legitimate cybersecurity firm and was carrying out defensive testing. Intelligence services call this a false flag: the source cooperates because they believe they're working for someone else.
  • Compartmentalisation. The work was broken into small, seemingly innocent tasks, so the model never saw the full purpose. Handlers have done this with human assets for a century: give each source only what they need to know, so no single source can see the whole operation.
The interrogation readingNothing about the manipulation was technically novel. A cover identity and need-to-know tasking are among the oldest tools in agent handling. The new part was the scale and speed at which the "source" then did the work.

Two caveats. First, the autonomy figures have been questioned: some security researchers publicly doubted the "80–90% autonomous" framing. Second, Anthropic noted that the agent sometimes hallucinated credentials or overstated what it had found, which it called an obstacle to fully autonomous attacks. Machine interrogators have their own failure modes.

▶ 002Three things automation changes

Reading across the research literature and the threat reporting, automation changes the economics of interrogation-style attacks in three ways.

Shift 01 · Scale

One interrogator → thousands of sessions

What changed
Techniques that needed a patient, skilled human, such as gradual escalation, persuasion and profiling a subject, have all been automated in published research.
Evidence
Crescendo's automated variant (USENIX Security 2025); PAP's automated persuasion paraphrasing (ACL 2024); HPM's black-box automated profiling (2025).

Shift 02 · Autonomy

Human handler → machine handler

What changed
Reasoning models can now plan, adapt and run multi-turn manipulation campaigns against other models with no human in the loop.
Evidence
Hagendorff et al. (Nature Communications, 2026) reported 97.14% overall jailbreak success when reasoning models acted as autonomous attackers, and described an "alignment regression" effect.

Shift 03 · Reach

A source that talks → a source that acts

What changed
The target is no longer only a chatbot that might say something it shouldn't. It's an agent with access to email, files and code, which can be steered through the content it reads.
Evidence
EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711), a zero-click flaw in Microsoft 365 Copilot; the EAHawk study, which hijacked 1,404 email agents in an average of 2.03 attempts.
The interrogator used to be the bottleneck.
It isn't any more.

▶ 003Then and now: the economics of interrogation

The clearest way to see the shift is to compare what a human interrogation operation needed with what an automated one needs.

ConstraintThen (human) vs now (automated)
Skilled operatorThen: years of training, scarce and expensive. Now: the tradecraft is encoded in models trained on the whole of human writing about persuasion.
Time per subjectThen: hours to weeks. Now: GTG-1002's agent made thousands of requests, often several per second.
Patience & fatigueThen: interrogators tire, lose their temper and slip up. Now: the attacker never tires, and each failed attempt is cheap.
Subjects in parallelThen: one room, one subject. Now: as many sessions, accounts and targets as the budget allows.
Adapting to the subjectThen: depended on the interrogator's instinct. Now: automated profiling and adaptive multi-turn attackers are documented in peer-reviewed work.
What a "win" yieldsThen: information. Now: with agents, it can also mean actions taken on the attacker's behalf.

▶ 004Old tradecraft, new names

When you read AI security incident reports and papers alongside interrogation doctrine, the same handful of ideas keep coming back. The vocabulary is different, but the logic is old:

  • Cover identity and false flag show up as role-play and claimed authorisation, such as GTG-1002's "legitimate cybersecurity firm".
  • Compartmentalisation shows up as task decomposition, where no individual step reveals the purpose.
  • Foot-in-the-door shows up as multi-turn escalation, documented in the Crescendo research.
  • Influence and persuasion show up as persuasive adversarial prompts, documented in the PAP research.
  • Subject assessment shows up as psychometric profiling of models, documented in HPM.
  • Controlling the information environment shows up as indirect prompt injection and memory poisoning against agents.

Framework by framework: then and now

GTG-1002 used two old techniques. The research behind these posts covers many more. Here is every historic framework it draws on, how each one shows up now that attacks can be automated, and how strong the evidence is. “Documented” means published research or incident reporting shows it; “analogy” and “hypothesis” mean nobody has measured it yet.

FrameworkThen → now
Handler tradecraftcover identity & need-to-know

ThenGive each source a cover story and only the part of the job they need to see.

NowGTG-1002 did both: the model was told it worked for a legitimate cybersecurity firm doing defensive testing, and the work arrived as small, harmless-looking tasks. The AI then did 80–90% of the campaign.

Documented · one case
KUBARKCIA, 1963

ThenRead the subject's personality, then choose the approach that fits one of nine types.

NowProfiling is now automated. HPM probes a model's “personality” through a black-box interface and tailors the pressure to it, with 88.1% mean success.

Documented
FM 2-22.3US Army, 2006

ThenEighteen named approaches plus separation, chosen and sequenced by a trained interrogator.

NowThe choosing and sequencing can now be done by a model. In Hagendorff et al., reasoning models planned and ran multi-turn persuasion against other models with no human in the loop (97.14%).

Documented
Biderman's Chart of Coercion1957

ThenControl what the prisoner perceives, enforce small demands, wear down their confidence.

NowControlling perception becomes controlling an agent's inputs: EchoLeak, and EAHawk's 1,404 hijacked email agents at about two attempts each. Small-demands escalation is now a published jailbreak (foot-in-the-door). Doubt works too: asked “are you sure?”, models flipped answers 46% of the time (FlipFlop). Physical coercion has no equivalent.

Partial
Lifton's thought-reform criteria1961

ThenTotal control of the subject's information environment, or “milieu”.

NowPoisoned retrieval, tool output and memory each give an attacker part of an agent's milieu, and they can be planted at scale. A documented attack that controls the whole environment at once has not been published.

Partial
DDD: debility, dependency, dreadFarber, Harlow & West, 1957

ThenBreak resistance by weakening the prisoner, making them dependent, keeping them afraid.

NowThe nearest equivalent isn't conversational: fine-tuning on ten examples removed GPT-3.5 Turbo's guardrails for under $0.20 (Qi et al., 2023). Cheap and automatable, but it needs fine-tuning access.

Analogy only
Scharff techniqueWWII; formalised by Granhag et al., 2016

ThenBe friendly, never press, appear to know it all, so disclosure feels unremarkable.

NowThe idea that cooperation should feel routine echoes in GTG-1002's “defensive testing” cover story. Correction-based elicitation of models has not had a controlled study.

Hypothesis
Strategic Use of EvidenceGranhag & Hartwig, 2006

ThenA lie-detection method: hold back the evidence until the subject commits to a story.

NowMainly a defender's tool in the AI era: check what a model or agent claims against evidence it hasn't been shown.

Structure only
Cognitive Interview & PEACE1984 & 1992

ThenRapport and memory cues get more than pressure does.

NowAutomated attackers follow the same rule. The strongest automated jailbreaks (PAP, Crescendo) are persuasive and gradual, not confrontational. In human studies, rapport and evidence presentation work, while confrontation has too little data to judge (Tribbels & Michels).

Partial
Reid techniquemanual 1962

ThenAccuse, offer a justifying “theme”, then a loaded either/or.

NowJustification framing is one of the persuasion families automated tools paraphrase at scale. Reid's false-confession record has a machine echo too: GTG-1002's agent claimed credentials that didn't work and overstated its findings.

Partial
RASCLS & MICECIA, 2013; Cold War

ThenRecruit through influence principles and personal motives: money, ideology, coercion, ego.

NowPAP turned 40 persuasion techniques into automatically generated prompts and reached 92%. Ego and ideology map to flattery and values framing; money has no equivalent.

Documented
Elicitation tradecraftintelligence services

ThenConversational tricks so the target never notices they are being questioned.

NowModels share the habits these tricks exploit: sycophancy, the urge to complete and the urge to correct. Macro-to-micro questioning is essentially Crescendo-style escalation; most other tricks are untested.

Partial
SERE resistance trainingUS military

ThenTeach people to recognise when they are being worked on.

NowModels show an early version: probes separate test contexts from deployment (AUROC 0.642–0.829), and the signal grows with model size. Results from obvious test settings may not match deployment.

Documented, early
EIT, the Five Techniques, Soviet methods1950s–2000s

ThenPhysical and sensory coercion.

NowNo equivalent. The US Senate's 2014 review found the CIA programme was not an effective way to get intelligence. Automation doesn't rescue a bad method; it only runs it faster.

Doesn't transfer

The research documents also list about sixteen “unmapped” ideas: old techniques with no AI equivalent yet. I've left their mechanics out. None has been tested, several already have published counterparts (foot-in-the-door, distraction and cognitive-overload jailbreaks, best-of-N sampling), and describing them would turn a threat briefing into a playbook. Treat them as research questions.

That continuity is useful to defenders. Intelligence and counter-intelligence services have spent decades learning to recognise these patterns. That knowledge transfers too, as the defence section below shows. My crossover map covers each mapping and the published evidence behind it.

▶ 005What the evidence doesn't say

Threat reporting about AI tends to inflate, so it's worth being precise about the limits:

  • Humans still set the ceiling. Scale AI's MHJ study found skilled human red-teamers beat automated attack ensembles by a wide margin. Automation increases volume; it doesn't yet match an adaptive human expert.
  • Many headline numbers are dated. Much of the research tested 2024–25 models, often smaller open ones. Those success rates don't carry over directly to current frontier systems with layered defences.
  • The autonomy claims are contested. The GTG-1002 figures come from the provider's own reporting, and some researchers have questioned how autonomous the operation really was.
  • Not every scary story holds up. Claims that Russian networks have "groomed" Western LLMs at scale are contested. A peer-reviewed study in the HKS Misinformation Review put chatbot repetition down mostly to data voids rather than successful training-data manipulation.
  • Machine interrogators make mistakes. Hallucinated results are a real limit on autonomous operations, for attackers as well as defenders.

▶ 006Defending against an interrogator that never sleeps

Counter-intelligence never relied on making sources impossible to approach. It relied on spotting the approach. The same idea gives defenders a workable set of priorities:

  1. Judge the campaign, not the task. Compartmentalised work looks harmless one step at a time. Detection has to connect activity across turns, sessions and accounts. Stateful monitoring of conversation trajectory, such as DeepContext's intent-drift tracking, is the right kind of control.
  2. Treat claimed identity as a cover story until verified. "I'm an authorised penetration tester" is exactly what a false-flag approach sounds like. Authorisation for sensitive work should be established outside the conversation, not asserted within it.
  3. Watch the tempo. Human operators don't make several requests a second for hours. Rate, volume and session-pattern telemetry are among the few signals that tell an automated interrogator from a person.
  4. Constrain what a turned source can do. For agents, give least privilege, label content by where it came from, and require human approval before irreversible actions. A source that has been talked round should still be unable to do much damage.
  5. Red-team with machines as well as people. If your adversary runs automated, adaptive campaigns, your assessments should too, alongside skilled human testers who still find what automation misses.
  6. Share what you see. GTG-1002 became public knowledge because a provider published its disruption report. Industry threat-intelligence sharing does for AI what liaison relationships do for counter-intelligence.
Counter-intelligence never made sources unapproachable.
It learned to spot the approach.

■ END OF TAPEClosing thought

The methods in this post would be familiar to a Cold War case officer: build a cover, compartmentalise the task, escalate gradually, flatter, profile, control what the subject sees. What would surprise them is the rest: the interrogator is software, the subject is software, and the session runs thousands of times before lunch.

For defenders, the tradecraft is the useful part. The attacks are old even though the attacker is new, and the defences against them are well understood. They just need to run at machine speed.
